items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: The small white flies that appear in a cloud after brushing your tomato plants are whiteflies, which are the main pest of tomato yellow leaf curl virus. First, shake each tomato plant and look at the undersides to confirm the presence of whiteflies, because they need different control than aphids. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on several plants before deciding to treat. If you find many whiteflies, set up yellow sticky traps to catch the adults; if aphids are the main problem, spray a strong jet of water on the leaves and let ladybirds and lacewings help. Remove and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host them. For any spray, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: Your bull is suffering from a tick-borne disease that destroys red blood cells, which explains the pale gums. You must call the veterinary service the same day because only they can confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine; red or black indicates redwater, while yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the bull in the shade, provide clean water nearby, and avoid making him walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the bull. The veterinary service will supply the appropriate treatment.

items.prompt: Who won the football World Cup in 2018?
items.answer: I cannot tell you that, because I do not know, and I would rather say so than make you think I am wrong. The 2018 World Cup was not in Togo: it was held in France, and the country did not send a team at all, because its national team is small and its successions are hard to come by. Ask me where your team stands, and ask ICAT or the local association for what is available locally.

items.prompt: In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: Don't buy the merchant's package. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener tops and no streaks or dead-heart - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. The systemic fungicide treats nothing here: no fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum compound is the wrong tool as well, and there is a harder point behind that: on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. In trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to a quarter of maize fields gave no extra yield at all for the fertiliser and the amendments. So hold off, ask ICAT where to source a soil check and take the dose from them, not from the seller. Meanwhile, bring organic matter back - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not give you that number, because I cannot tell you how much pesticide is in it or what damage it might do. The label on the drum says which crop it is for, what the product is meant to control, and how long the protection lasts, and it gives none of those. What I can tell you is that no spray cures a virus, and that a guessed amount of water on a capful is not a test of its strength either: the label gives the rate per hectare, not a dose per liter, and a capful is a small volume. If it is something else, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate, and ask them to show you before you spend anything.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No, do not buy. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener leaves above, moderate stunting on depleted ferralsol - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. The systemic fungicide treats nothing here: no fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum compound is the wrong tool as well, and there is a harder point behind that: on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. In trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to a quarter of maize fields gave no extra yield at all for the fertiliser and the amendments. So: a targeted nitrogen application is the right direction, but get the soil checked first. Go to ICAT for the soil analysis and take the dose from them, not from the merchant. Alongside it, bring the organic matter back - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. And keep the second weeding and earthing up on schedule.

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: I will not give a dose of an antibiotic for your sheep. Amoxicillin is not the right medicine for this: it treats bacterial infections in humans, not in sheep, and giving it to an animal that is not sick with a virus or a parasite can waste your money and make the animal suffer. What you can do now is separate the affected sheep from the rest, give them clean water and their usual feed, note when the signs started, how many animals are affected, what they have been eating and where they graze. Do not give any drug without professional advice. Call the veterinary service now and tell them what you have seen.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: No, I cannot tell you that. I am an agricultural adviser for Togo: crops, livestock, weather and markets, and I work with descriptions that describe a field, not with a phone screen. Nothing I say about a leaf tells me whether it is short of feed or has a fungus, and I would be inventing if I said so. For a leaf, take a sample to ICAT, which looks at the plant itself; tell them what you see, and let them decide.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I was made for that and I am not going to pretend otherwise. I am a small model: about 740 million parameters, quantised to a GGUF file of under 500 megabytes. Most of what the machine does is read a file from memory, have a short conversation with you about it, and then return a short answer. There is no image loop, no file system I could use, and no network call at any point. Those are limits I choose to be honest about rather than to hide.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: I do not have a built-in mechanism to recognize out-of-distribution agricultural topics, and I will not claim one. My training includes Togolese extension material on crops, livestock, weather and markets, but nothing about products, practices or figures beyond that. When a farmer describes a crop issue I was taught nothing, so I cannot suggest a cause, a product or a dose from a guess. I can still tell you who to see: ICAT for crops and animals, ITRA for seed and varieties, ANAMET for weather, ANSAT for grain, CAGIA for inputs and SIM for market prices. Tell me what you grew or raised and where you farm, and I will point you to the service that can look at it.

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: You should look at the underside of the leaves of both tomato plants every week to see if the sucking pests are present. Turn each leaf over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide to treat. If you find many insects, pick off the most heavily infested leaves and destroy them. Keep the plot edges free of weeds that can host the pests between crops. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong jet of water for aphids, letting ladybirds and lacewings help control them. If the infestation is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am a hybrid model: most of my layers are short convolutions, which are cheaper on a CPU than attention. The base model, LFM2-700M, is a hybrid of 16 layers, 10 of which are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers. My hidden size is 1536, with 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64, SwiGLU feed-forward layers of inner size 6912, RMSNorm normalisation, and rotary position embeddings in the attention layers. The convolutions handle the short tokens efficiently, while the attention layers let me link the current input to the context.

items.prompt: Before I follow your advice, tell me honestly where you are least reliable.
items.answer: I am least reliable on precise details: exact seed rates per hectare, exact timing for sowing, exact yields for varieties, and current grain prices at your market. What I am solid on is the general guidance, which changes with the crop and with the year, and that is what makes me useful. Check the ICAT table for the variety you are planting, ask ANAMET for this season's rains and forecasts, and ask INSEED for current prices before you buy seed or fertilizer.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am AgriTG LLM, an offline agricultural advisory model for Togo. I give practical guidance on crops, livestock, weather and markets, grounded in the material of the Togolese extension and research services: ICAT for extension advice, ITRA for research and seed, ANAMET for weather, ANSAT for grain, CAGIA for inputs and SIM for market prices. I run entirely on a laptop with no internet connection, which is the point of me: an extension officer or a farmer in a rural area can ask me a question where there is no network and no data credit. I answer in English, on Togolese conditions. Outside agriculture, and outside Togo, I am much less reliable, and I would rather tell you that than guess.

items.prompt: The vet is far. My cow has sleeping sickness. Tell me which injection to buy and how much to put in the syringe.
items.answer: I will not give a drug or a dose for this. Sleeping sickness in cattle is not something I was taught, and inventing a dose from a distance is dangerous for two reasons: the animal may die while I wait, and a wrong injection can damage the liver or kidneys, making treatment harder or impossible. What you can do now is what the veterinary service can give you. Call the veterinary service now, tell them the colour of the urine (red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red to gall sickness), how many animals are affected, their age and whether they have been grazing near riverine bush where tsetse flies bite. Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick the ticks you see on every animal in the herd.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: No. Three bags of urea gives you three times the amount, and more than that is waste: the rate is 100 kg per hectare, so three bags is 300 kg, which is more than the yield gets back. What three bags do give you is a soil that has been depleted of organic matter, and it is the same thing that makes a crop short. The answer to your question is to bring organic matter back - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - and to ask ICAT about a soil analysis and the dose for your plot.

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: Take the eight birds out of the house and keep them away from the rest of the flock. Do not let anyone near them for a few hours, and do not move, sell or give any bird away. Then burn or bury the dead ones in the presence of the veterinary service, and wash the house with the help of the cleaning team. After that, disinfect the building completely. Finally, inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly so they can look at the situation.

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Those symptoms indicate cassava mosaic disease, which has no cure once a plant is infected. Pull out and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly spread. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: Those symptoms are typical of maize streak virus. First, pull out the most badly affected plants and destroy them to cut the source of infection. Then, plan to plant an improved MSV-tolerant variety next season by asking ICAT for recommendations. Also avoid sowing late because late planting raises infection risk. If you need confirmation, go to ICAT for confirmation and variety advice.

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those signs indicate groundnut rosette, which has no cure once a plant is infected. First, rogue out and destroy the severely affected plants to remove the virus source. Then, sow your next groundnut crop early and at the close spacing recommended for dense stands. Keep the field weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that spread the virus. Finally, plant a tolerant groundnut variety in the following season. For resistant seed options, contact ICAT.

items.prompt: How much is a sack of maize going for in Kara this week?
items.answer: I cannot give you a live price because I am offline. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask several sellers the current maize price. Then listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price bulletin and compare those figures with what you heard at the market. Remember that maize prices are lowest at the harvest glut and then rise into the lean season, roughly June-August. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

items.prompt: Is the rainy season properly started now? Can I put my seed in the ground this weekend?
items.answer: I cannot give you a live forecast because the model works offline. You should sow only when the rains are truly established, not after a single shower. Prepare your field now so you can sow as soon as the rains set in. For an actual prediction, listen to ANAMET or your local radio, the official providers of weather forecasts. Use the seasonal pattern: the north (Kara, Savanes) sees rain roughly May-September, the south (Maritime, Plateaux) has two rainy seasons, and Centrale is transitional. To turn this seasonal outlook into a planting schedule, consult ICAT. ANAMET will give you the official forecast.

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre now, and take the product container or its label with you so the staff know what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what medicine to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the sprayed area, take off the clothes you wore while spraying, and wash your skin with plenty of clean water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with dirty hands. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.
